candidates.name: Scott Monument
candidates.content: Sir Walter Scott (1771-1832) re-invented Scotland. In the late Georgian era, he popularised tales of its medieval and Jacobean tumults, and created the clan tartans you buy on Princes St. This grand Gothic memorial, part cathedral

candidates.name: National Galleries of Scotland: National
candidates.price: Free, charges for major temporary exhibitions
candidates.content: This holds much of Scotland's fine artwork from Renaissance to 20th century, with changing exhibitions. These rotate seasonally, so an exhibition put on for the Festival typically stays to the end of the year, allowing quieter tim

candidates.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Modern One
candidates.content: The original modern art gallery, established in 1960, was in the Botanic Gardens. In 1895 it moved into this neoclassical building, originally a refuge for fatherless children, and in 1999 it expanded across the road into the neoc

candidates.name: Edinburgh Castle
candidates.price: Adult £19.50, child (7-15) £11.40, conc £15.50, Historic Scotland / English Heritage / Cadw free
candidates.content: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. High

candidates.name: Camera Obscura
candidates.content: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight

candidates.name: Gladstone's Land
candidates.price: Adult £10, conc £8.50, child £6, NTS / NT free
candidates.content: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only spa

candidates.name: Writers' Museum
candidates.content: This museum, in a tall house built in 1622, celebrates three Scottish literary giants: Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. From 1719 the close was the residence of the widow of the 1st Earl of Stair, who ord

candidates.name: St Giles
candidates.content: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays

candidates.name: Museum of Childhood
candidates.content: Concepts and imagery of childhood are ever-changing. See if you can find your (or your grandparents') old toys in the collection, and your place in history.

candidates.name: The Peoples' Story Museum
candidates.content: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised la

candidates.name: Canongate Kirk
candidates.hours: Open Sun afternoon, otherwise erratic; Services Sun 10:30
candidates.content: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to In

candidates.name: Scottish Parliament
candidates.hours: Mon Fri Sat and public holidays 10AM-5PM, Tue-Thu 9AM-6:30PM
candidates.content: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets T

candidates.name: Dynamic Earth
candidates.content: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

candidates.name: Holyrood Palace
candidates.hours: Nov-Mar Thu-Mon 9:30AM - 4:30PM, Apr-Oct Thu-Mon (& daily Jul-Sep) 9:30AM - 6PM
candidates.content: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the g

candidates.name: National Library of Scotland
candidates.content: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the str

candidates.name: National Museum of Scotland
candidates.content: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and des

candidates.name: St Cecilia's Hall
candidates.content: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Tromp

candidates.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
candidates.content: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired Brideshead Revisited and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fell

candidates.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
candidates.content: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

candidates.name: Fruitmarket
candidates.content: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

candidates.name: Museum on the Mound
candidates.content: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own bank

candidates.name: Craigmillar Castle
candidates.content: Extensive ruin of a medieval castle, built from the 14th century and abandoned in the 18th. Here was hatched the plot to murder Lord Darnley, the inconvenient husband of Mary Queen of Scots. He was blown up at Kirk O'Field (now th

candidates.name: Lauriston Castle
candidates.content: This 1590s tower house was extended in the 1820s and housed a series of prosperous families. It passed into council ownership in 1926 and the interior has been preserved in its last occupants' plush Edwardian style. Visit by pre-b

candidates.name: Calton Hill
candidates.content: This is the stubby crag just east of Princes Street: a short stroll up it commands great views. The "National Monument", a memorial to Scots killed in the Napoleonic Wars, was an attempt to out-do the Parthenon in Athens but the m

candidates.name: Royal Scottish Academy
candidates.content: An august neo-classical building on The Mound, fronting onto Princes St, and its main function is to be confused with the National Gallery behind. The RSA is a separate organisation promoting contemporary Scottish art. The buildin

candidates.name: Princes Street Gardens
candidates.content: The west portion fills the valley beyond the Mound, spanning the railway tracks to the foot of castle crag. The east portion is the terrace around the Scott Monument. They were laid out in the 1820s as private gardens for resident

candidates.name: St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral
candidates.content: This stonking great neo-Gothic church was completed in 1879, designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, with the towers added in 1917. It's the senior Episcopal church in Scotland, within the Anglican tradition of bishops (and much els

candidates.name: St Mary's Metropolitan Cathedral
candidates.content: The Roman Catholic Cathedral was established as a chapel in 1814 and became a cathedral in 1886 for the archdiocese of Edinburgh and St Andrews. It was designed by James Gillespie Graham in neo-perpendicular style and has undergon

candidates.name: Edinburgh International Festival
candidates.content: The original that spawned all the rest. Founded in 1947 and still seen as more "high-brow" than any of its offspring. Surprisingly, tickets are often priced more reasonably than for many Fringe shows. Some events have preview perf

candidates.name: Edinburgh Military Tattoo
candidates.content: One of the iconic images of Edinburgh for millions worldwide is the yearly Tattoo, kilted pipers skirling below the battlements of Edinburgh Castle. Although tickets sell out well in advance, persevering individuals are likely to

candidates.name: Edinburgh Festival Fringe
candidates.content: As the name might suggest, this festival developed on the fringe of the main International Festival and offers more alternative performances, with an emphasis on comedy and avant-garde; it is now the largest arts festival in the w

candidates.name: Edinburgh Jazz and Blues Festival
candidates.content: Festival of about 150 concerts in 11 venues.

candidates.name: Edinburgh International Book Festival
candidates.content: Takes place in a temporary village of marquees at Charlotte Square Gardens (West End of George Street, New Town).

candidates.name: Edinburgh Art Festival
candidates.content: Some permanent outdoor commissions which can be seen all year, and temporary exhibitions and events during the festival.

candidates.name: Edinburgh Mela
candidates.content: Multicultural festival held in Leith.

candidates.name: Edinburgh International Television Festival
candidates.content: Predominantly a "closed shop" for industry professionals only.

candidates.name: Hibernian FC
candidates.content: The "Hibs" play soccer in the Premiership, Scotland's top tier. The all-seater stadium, capacity 24,000, is at the south edge of Leith. Hibs have played at Easter Road since 1893; in 2000 the pronounced slope of the ground was lev

candidates.name: Usher Hall
candidates.content: The city's main concert hall, capacity 2200, and home to the Royal Scottish National Orchestra. It was completed in 1914, funded by Andrew Usher the whisky distiller and blender.

candidates.name: The Grange
candidates.content: This is the usual home ground for the Scottish national team, the Saltires. They play 50-over and 20-over matches but not five-day Tests. Gen!us Grange play in the domestic leagues.

candidates.name: Murrayfield Stadium
candidates.content: The main stadium has a capacity of 67,000 and hosts all Scottish rugby internationals. The premier tournament is the Six Nations held each February-March: in odd-numbered years, Scotland hosts Wales, Ireland and Italy, and in even

candidates.name: Heart of Midlothian
candidates.content: Hearts aka "the Jambos" and "the Gorgie Boys" play soccer in the Scottish Premiership, the top tier. Their home ground Tynecastle Park (capacity 20,000, all-seater) is a mile west of Haymarket station in the Gorgie area of the cit

candidates.name: Degree Show
candidates.content: Around the end of May the Edinburgh College of Art opens its doors and exhibits the works on art, design and architecture of their students. A similar event, the Masters Degree Show, takes place in August as part of the Edinburgh

candidates.name: Samhuinn Fire Festival
candidates.content: Fire Festival marking the beginning of winter (evening of October 31). Procession and enacted fight between the King of Summer and Prince of Winter with great accompanying percussion.

candidates.name: Beltane Fire Festival
candidates.content: Fire Festival marking the beginning of summer (evening of April 30). The festival has its origins in the pre-Christian Celtic festival of the same name, which was held to herald the coming of spring and to celebrate the fertility

candidates.name: Hidden Door
candidates.content: Annual non-profit art, music, theatre, etc. event taking place in unused spaces in the city that change from year to year. End of May/beginning of June.

candidates.name: Edinburgh International Film Festival
candidates.content: Now moved to June from its former slot in August, so that it no longer clashes with all the others! Centred around the Filmhouse Cinema on Lothian Road, though other cinemas take part too. In 2022 it is back in August, but it is n

candidates.name: The Edinburgh Dungeon
candidates.content: "Haunted House" experience, where you take a 70 min tour through 11 shows and 2 rides loosely based on Scotland's horrible history: William Wallace, Mary King's Ghost, cannibal Sawney Bean, Burke and Hare and more.

candidates.name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
candidates.content: Tour of the history and craft of whisky distilling, with expert guides - the basic or "silver" tour works well for beginners. They have a huge selection; the core of it is the 3384 bottles collected by Brazilian whisky enthusiast

candidates.name: Sheep Heid Inn
candidates.content: 18th-century pub, with implausible claims to date from 1360, and perhaps named for the village slaughter-ground. In 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie's army camped outside for a month and he held a Council of War here, to good effect as

candidates.name: The Oxford Bar
candidates.content: Trad drouthy Scottish pub, often a setting in the Ian Rankin "Inspector Rebus" novels.

candidates.name: Port of Leith Distillery
candidates.content: This converted biscuit factory is a vertical distillery - water is pumped just once up the nine-storey building and gravity does the rest, more efficient than multiple intermediate pumping. There's a rooftop bar, and they market S

candidates.name: Scotch Malt Whisky Society
candidates.content: Connoisseur whisky-drinkers' private club, with other branches on Queen St and in Glasgow, trying to convey old-money opulence and exclusivity without snootiness and froideur. If you've genuinely got a nose for the good stuff and

candidates.name: Teuchters Landing
candidates.content: Friendly pub with food in a former cruise liner waiting room. Lots of outside tables by the water so a great choice for a sunny afternoon. They have another branch in the West End.

candidates.name: The Cask & Barrel
candidates.content: This often features in the novels of Christopher Brookmyre as the pub where journalist "Jack Parlabane" gets tip-offs from the police. The Cask is a proper boozer with a wide selection of Real Ale plus draft and bottled lagers and

candidates.name: The Cumberland Bar
candidates.hours: Mon-Thu 4:30-11PM, Fri Sat noon-midnight, Sun noon-11PM
candidates.content: Readers of Alexander McCall Smith's 44 Scotland Street will recognise this literary haunt. It's a traditional pub popular with New Town locals, students, the suits from local offices, pretty much everyone in fact. Gets very busy i

candidates.name: Doctors
candidates.content: Now a Belhaven pub, this is a welcoming place with good ales and food. It was a few yards from the former Royal Infirmary, within bleep range and sprinting distance for the junior doctors.

candidates.name: The Kilderkin
candidates.content: Fair selection of cask ales and whisky, the food is so-so and the warmth of welcome varies. This is the original of a chain that now includes The Windsor on Elm Row, Blue Blazer on Spittal St and Bennets at Tolcross.

candidates.name: Bennets Bar
candidates.content: A good old-fashioned pub, now part of Kilderkin group, with a wide selection of real ale and whisky. It is traditionally the place for pre / post-theatre drinks, with the Kings Theatre.

candidates.name: The Regent
candidates.content: LGBT+ and straight-friendly bar with real ale.

candidates.name: Nobles
candidates.content: Elegantly decorated cafe bar with good food.

candidates.name: Nauticus
candidates.content: Nautical-themed pub with dark panelling, they have beer but are mainly a whisky and cocktail bar. No food.

candidates.name: Lind and Lime Distillery
candidates.content: They make gin, named for James Lind the Scottish surgeon who advocated the use of limes to treat and prevent scurvy at sea. In 1747 he conducted the world's first controlled clinical trial, comparing six different remedies for scu

candidates.name: Cafe Piccante
candidates.content: Unashamed specialists in late-night greasy food, friendly staff and a DJ at weekends. The burgers are a stand-out and deep-fried mars bars are available for tourists.

candidates.name: Whiski
candidates.content: A bit touristy, but a good choice for Scottish food, drink and music. Hundreds of whiskies available, bar staff happy to advise. Live music every night from 9:30PM, try to sit up front for this.

candidates.name: The Elephant House
candidates.content: Consistently good coffee and light bites, cafe is full of university and creative types; JK Rowling wrote much of the first Harry Potter book here. And that alas is the problem: it's become part of the Potter circus, every half ho

candidates.name: Malvarosa
candidates.content: Good selection of tapas and slick service.

candidates.name: Word of Mouth Bistro
candidates.content: Pleasant small bistro for breakfast or lunch. They have another branch in Morningside.

candidates.name: Snax
candidates.content: A small fast-food joint, limited seating. The food is cheap and edible, with a decent vegetarian selection.

candidates.name: The Palmerston
candidates.content: Chicly decorated restaurant and bakery in a former bank, the menu changes daily.

candidates.name: The Piemaker
candidates.content: This has a wide range of delicious pies and savoury pastries, piping hot. They're mostly a takeaway and don't deliver, but have a few seats inside.

candidates.name: Kebab Mahal
candidates.content: Good halal curries, kebabs and tandooris, no alcohol.

candidates.name: The Original Mosque Kitchen
candidates.content: Inexpensive chicken or vegetable curry. A favorite with generations of Edinburgh University students for its cost and portion sizes.

candidates.name: Tempting Tattie
candidates.content: Inexpensive takeaway for trad baked potatoes.

candidates.name: Kampong Ah Lee
candidates.content: Tasty Malaysian dishes such as Roti Canai, Satay, Nasi Lemak, Laksa and Rendang.

candidates.name: St James Quarter
candidates.content: Shopping centre which opened in 2021, replacing the tired St James Centre, includes John Lewis department store, and 3 floors of mid- and up-market chain stores. Also here are the W Hotel, Roomzzz aparthotel and several restaurant

candidates.name: Waverley Market
candidates.content: Upmarket mainstream shops in a covered mall above Waverley station.

candidates.name: Hing Sing
candidates.content: Chinese supermarket with food items from across south-east Asia, plus crockery and cooking utensils. Great for those hard-to-find ingredients but even items stocked by mainstream supermarkets are often better value here.

candidates.name: Asda
candidates.content: The biggest local supermarket, with pharmacy, opticians, travel money and filling station.

candidates.name: Scotmid Coop
candidates.content: Convenience supermarket in Tolcross.

december.text: Edinburgh is a year-round destination. It gets very busy around New Year (known in Scotland as Hogmanay), the Six Nations rugby internationals in Feb / March, and particularly during the Fringe Festivals in August - book accommodation well in advance for these.

Edinburgh in the winter festive season is also huge with various concerts and other activities taking place starting a couple of weeks before Christmas and running up to a week into January. Princes Street Gardens play host to a Big Wheel, outdoor ice rink and various festive markets. As in most of the rest of Scotland

Edinburgh has been established as a tourist destination for centuries, so there is a huge choice of accommodation available for travellers. If you're planning a visit during festival time (Aug), around Christmas and New Year, or on the weekend of a Scotland home game in the 6-nations Rugby (Mar/Apr, 2 or 3 matches per
